news_drafts.headline: Luton forecasts £2.83m overspend on £54.39m high needs budget for 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Luton Council's special educational needs budget is forecast to overspend by £2.83m in 2026/27, according to the first quarterly budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) for the year. The report went to the council's Scrutiny Finance Review Group on 26 October 2026.

All of it falls in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The allocation is £54.39m. The forecast already takes account of £0.88m moved into high needs from the Schools Block, a separate part of the schools grant, a transfer approved in January 2026.

The report says the forecast "continues to be driven by demand-led pressures". It also describes it as "subject to significant uncertainty". It says national SEND reforms have led to a "substantial increase" in requests for Education, Health and Care Needs Assessments, which are assessments of a child's needs for support. The report says these are expected to put further pressure on high needs and on related services paid for from the council's main General Fund budget.

news_drafts.headline: Luton procurement exemptions reach 680 in 2025/26, up from 321 in 2023/24, mostly children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Requests to bypass Luton Council's normal buying rules (exemptions to standing orders) rose to 680 in 2025/26, from 321 in 2023/24 and 566 the year before, the Audit & Governance Committee is told in its annual procurement report. The council approved 471 of them, with £41.8m in approved value.

Children, Families & Education accounted for 311 of the requests, 46% of the total. Its requests were worth £40.6m, 57% by value, and the council approved 244 of them (78%) and £21.4m of the value (53%). The report attributes the increase largely to residential care and foster care placements, out-of-borough school places for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), and home-to-school transport. Rejections also rose, to 209 from 119 in 2023/24. About 44% were for administrative errors and 17% for missing conflict-of-interest declarations.

The council has set up a Passenger Transport Services Framework, a compliant route for buying home-to-school transport, which accounted for about £2.6m of exemption value in 2025/26. The paper says this is expected to "significantly reduce" future requests in that area. Members are asked to acknowledge that the council's processes, commissioning arrangements and procurement policies need further review for residential care, foster care and out-of-borough school placements.

The committee also has the first-quarter budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget). Adult social care is forecasting a £1.7m overspend from demand and complexity, and the High Needs Block, the part of school funding for children with SEND, a £2.8m overspend even after an approved £880k transfer from the Schools Block. The corporate risks paper says the council balanced its 2026/27 budget without using reserves, helped by a 5% council tax rise and the government funding settlement, after a significant 2025/26 deficit that it did not size. It is pursuing a deficit recovery plan over two years.

On internal audit, of 349 recommendations followed up, 76% were fully implemented, 20% were in progress and 4% not yet started.

news_drafts.headline: Luton complaints handling falls short of 80% target despite quarterly improvement
news_drafts.lead: Luton's complaints performance reached 62.4% in-service-level agreement (in-SLA) in the year to March 2026, falling 17.6 percentage points short of the 80% target the council set for the first time in January. The council showed quarterly progress, rising from 60.8% in the first quarter to 65.5% in the fourth, and ombudsman compensation claims dropped 69% to £4,750. However, Children, Family & Education — the highest-risk area — saw complaints surge 54% to 216 while performance remained flat at 34.3% in-SLA, leaving cases unresolved at an average of 52.9 days against an 80% target. The council has committed to a dedicated recovery plan with weekly leadership review and targets of 60% in-SLA by the end of the second quarter and 75% by year-end, conditional on training completion and new platform implementation.

findings.headline: The committee is asked to support a review of the Personal Travel Budget element, moving away from fixed bandings
findings.detail: The paper recommends that the policy allow custom Personal Travel Budget arrangements where individual assessment confirms the award meets the assessed need, is practical for the family, and represents best use of funds. The stated reason is that fixed bandings currently restrict the council's ability to agree the most cost-effective form of assistance.
findings.matters: Replacing fixed PTB bandings with individually set awards is a policy change that alters how a council controls the unit cost of SEND travel, which peers facing similar pressures would want to track.
findings.quote: moving away from reliance on fixed bandings where this restricts the Council’s ability to agree the most appropriate and cost-effective form of travel assistance.

findings.headline: Statutory school-age rejections rose from 64 in 2024/25 to 141 in 2025/26, and appeals overturned rose from 24 to 52
findings.detail: The paper links the rise in rejections mainly to the form of transport offered, including moves from lone single-use taxi to multiple-occupancy minibus. It also notes that statutory school-age policy changes do not take effect until 2026-27, and that rejections on eligibility had fallen to 52 by 03.09.2026.
findings.matters: A rising overturn rate at appeal means initial decisions are being reversed at scale, which affects how far a council can rely on its forecast savings from changed transport arrangements.
findings.figures: School Age Rejections 64 (2024/25), 141 (2025/26), 52 (2026/27 as of 03.09.2026); Appeals received 75, 62, 15; Appeals overturned 24, 52, 8 (5 pending)
findings.quote: rising from 64 to 141, alongside a reduction in appeals from 75 to 62

findings.headline: Post-16 council-arranged transport placements fell from 111 in 2024 to 55 in 2026, while Personal Travel Budgets rose from 22 to 50
findings.detail: The paper reports a shift in how post-16 travel assistance is delivered, toward Personal Travel Budgets and away from council-arranged transport. The 2026 figures are provisional, with 28 applications still pending, and the paper says final uptake may change once those are determined.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this change in delivery mix against their own SEND transport contracts, since it moves spend from fleet and contracted placements to direct budgets.
findings.figures: Post-16 delivery type: Transport 111 (2024), 65 (2025), 55 (2026); PTB 22, 41, 50; MR 11, 19, 2; Pending applications 28 (2026); Total 144, 125, 135
findings.quote: Transport placements reduced from 111 in 2024 to 55 in 2026, while Personal Travel Budgets increased from 22 to 50 over the same period.

findings.headline: Public Health forecasting break-even position with £0.812m reserve drawdown to fund contractual inflation including three years of Agenda for Change pay increases rebasing the Sexual Health contract
findings.detail: Public Health is forecasting a break-even position assuming a £0.812m contribution from the Public Health reserve. The drawdown reflects a £0.5m contribution towards council-wide services delivering Public Health services and contractual inflation. Most significantly, the Sexual Health contract has been rebased to reflect three years of Agenda for Change pay increases.
findings.matters: Shows reserve depletion to balance budget and pressure from contracted pay award passthrough in externally-managed services, a structural cost driver
findings.figures: £0.812m reserve drawdown; £0.5m contribution to council services
findings.quote: The current forecast for Public Health is a break-even position, assuming a £0.812m contribution from the Public Health reserve. Reflecting a £0.5m contribution towards Council wide service delivering Public Health services and the contractual inflation, most significantly the rebasing of the Sexual Health contract, reflecting three years of Agenda for Change Pay increases.

findings.paper_title: 9. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2026-27 Quarter 1 Budget Monitoring Report
findings.headline: HRA external income forecast to exceed budget by £0.805m due to lower-than-anticipated Right to Buy sales retaining properties for rental income
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is forecast to underspend £0.301m overall. External income is forecast to exceed budget by £0.805m, mainly because Right to Buy sales are lower than anticipated, retaining more properties within the housing stock for rental income. Additional income is also expected from new homes coming into management. This income benefit more than offsets running expense overspends of £0.605m (primarily Responsive Repairs £0.705m from increased disrepair and compliance work).
findings.matters: Lower RtB sales and retained rental stock improve HRA financial sustainability; increased repairs costs are being offset by higher income, indicating stock condition pressures but good landlord income performance
findings.figures: £0.805m income above budget; £0.301m HRA underspend; £0.605m running expense overspend; Responsive Repairs £0.705m pressure
findings.quote: External income is forecast to exceed budget by £0.805m, mainly due to lower-than-anticipated Right to Buy sales, resulting in more properties being retained within the housing stock and generating rental income. Additional income is also expected from new homes coming into management during the year.
